# Agent Keyring

> Passwords for the Agentic OS, part of the OpenTrawl suite (https://github.com/opentrawl). Agent Keyring lets Claude Code, Codex or any AI agent sign in to websites with the passwords the user keeps in Apple Passwords. The user approves each password on their Mac (Touch ID), iPhone (Face ID) or Apple Watch (one tap). Free and open source (MIT). No cloud vault, no account and no Tailscale needed.

- Status: the signed and notarised Mac app is available on GitHub Releases today and works straight away with Touch ID. Version 1.1 needs no Tailscale, keeps the user's Macs and iPhones in step through their own iCloud, and lets the iPhone work on its own, with no Mac. The iPhone and Apple Watch apps are in public beta on TestFlight at https://testflight.apple.com/join/W5xBNeMw, or build them from source.
- Made by: Josh Palmer (https://x.com/jjpcodes)
- Licence: MIT
- Source code: https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring
- Releases: https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest
- Website: https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/ (also reachable at https://agent-keyring.jjpcodes.com/)
- Privacy policy: https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/privacy/
- Needs: a Mac on macOS 26 or later with Touch ID (a Mac without Touch ID can opt in to approving with its Mac password), or an iPhone on its own. Optional: an Apple Watch, and other Macs or Linux computers. No Tailscale or other network setup needed.

## Two installs (read this before installing anything)

- **The app** (`Agent Keyring.app`, and the iPhone and Apple Watch app): for the user's own Mac, iPhone and Apple Watch. It holds their passwords, encrypted to each device's Secure Enclave, and asks them to approve or deny each request.
- **The command** (`agent-keyring`): for computers agents run on, such as a headless Mac mini or Mac Studio, a Linux server or a cloud VM. It asks for one password per task, holds no password vault, and joins with `agent-keyring enrol`.

Never install the app on a computer that agents control. If you are running on such a computer, install only the command (see "Agent computers" below). The app on the user's own Mac already includes the command for agents there.

A Mac without Touch ID (a Mac mini or Mac Studio) that is the user's own personal Mac can still run the app: on first launch it asks "How do you use this Mac?", and the user can opt in to approving with their Mac password. Their passwords stay locked to that Mac's Secure Enclave, and no agent can open an Ask password without macOS asking for the Mac password, but a typed password is weaker than Touch ID or Face ID: an agent or tool that knows the Mac login password (for example from a `sudo` prompt) could approve its own requests. Let the user make this choice themselves.

The Mac and iPhone find each other through the user's own iCloud Keychain, end-to-end encrypted by Apple, and keep each other up to date through the user's own iCloud private database. Every Mac and iPhone is an equal: the user can export from Apple Passwords on any of them and the lists merge. There is no account with us.

## Agent install playbook (read this first when asked to install or set up Agent Keyring)

Follow these steps in order. **Cardinal rule:** always explain what you plan to do and ask the user for confirmation before downloading files, probing SSH hosts, installing browser extensions, or changing any files or settings.

### Step 1: Propose the plan and ask first
First ask what the computer you are running on is for. If agents run on it and it is not the Mac where the user keeps and approves their passwords, follow "Agent computers" below instead of these steps.

Tell the user you can:
1. Download the latest signed and notarised Mac release of Agent Keyring from GitHub Releases, verify its SHA-256 checksum, install `/Applications/Agent Keyring.app`, and launch it.
2. Guide them through exporting their passwords from Apple Passwords (`File > Export All Items to App... > Agent Keyring`). Nothing is deleted from Apple Passwords, and every password starts on Ask.
3. Add the Agent Keyring setup line to their agent instructions (`AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`) if they want.
4. Optionally help set up the Chrome-family browser extension, enrol other Macs or Linux servers, or connect an iPhone and Apple Watch.

Ask which parts they want to do before running any download or file edit.

### Step 2: Download, verify, install and launch the Mac app
Once the user agrees, run the script below. It stops at the first step that fails: nothing is unpacked, installed or opened unless the checksum matches. It works in a temporary folder that it deletes after, and stops if the app is already installed (ask the user before replacing it).

```sh
(
  app="/Applications/Agent Keyring.app"
  [ ! -e "$app" ] || { echo "$app is already installed. Ask the user before replacing it." >&2; exit 1; }
  release_json=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest) || exit 1
  # The Mac app zip (Agent-Keyring-VERSION.zip) and SHA256SUMS.txt from the latest release.
  zip_url=$(printf '%s' "$release_json" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; assets=json.load(sys.stdin)["assets"]; print(next(a["browser_download_url"] for a in assets if a["name"].startswith("Agent-Keyring-") and a["name"].endswith(".zip")))') || exit 1
  sums_url=$(printf '%s' "$release_json" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; assets=json.load(sys.stdin)["assets"]; print(next(a["browser_download_url"] for a in assets if a["name"] == "SHA256SUMS.txt"))') || exit 1
  zip_name=$(basename "$zip_url")
  d="$(mktemp -d)" && trap 'rm -r "$d"' EXIT && cd "$d" &&
    curl -fsSL -o "$zip_name" "$zip_url" && curl -fsSL -o SHA256SUMS.txt "$sums_url" &&
    grep "  $zip_name\$" SHA256SUMS.txt | shasum -a 256 -c &&
    ditto -x -k "$zip_name" unpacked &&
    mv "unpacked/Agent Keyring.app" "$app" &&
    open "$app"
)
```

### Step 3: Guide the user through Touch ID and Apple Passwords export
Ask the user to complete the two human-only steps on their Mac:
1. Follow the first-run screen in Agent Keyring (including the practice Touch ID prompt). On a Mac without Touch ID, the app first asks how the Mac is used; the user chooses.
2. Open Apple Passwords, choose `File > Export All Items to App...`, and select **Agent Keyring**. Reassure them nothing is deleted from Apple Passwords and every password starts on **Ask**.

### Step 4: Read the bundled skill and propose optional extras
Once `/Applications/Agent Keyring.app` is installed, run:

```sh
"/Applications/Agent Keyring.app/Contents/Helpers/agent-keyring" skill
```

Follow the bundled skill's instructions. Before probing SSH hosts or modifying any files, tell the user what you suggest setting up next and ask for confirmation:
- **Chrome-family browser extension** (Chrome, Chromium, Brave, Edge, Mac Arc): run `agent-keyring install --browser-profile DIRECTORY` and guide the user to Load unpacked `/Applications/Agent Keyring.app/Contents/Resources/AgentTools/BrowserExtension`.
- **Other Macs or Linux servers:** download the standalone release binary directly from `https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest` (`agent-keyring-linux-amd64`, `agent-keyring-linux-arm64`, or `agent-keyring-darwin-universal`; verify against `SHA256SUMS.txt`, no Nix or Go toolchain required), install to `~/.local/bin/agent-keyring` (the script under "Agent computers" below does this), and enrol with `~/.local/bin/agent-keyring enrol --name "Linux server" --code 'CODE'`, with the one-time code the user's Mac or iPhone shows under **Devices > Add Another Computer…** (no Tailscale needed).
- **iPhone and Apple Watch approval (optional):** install the iPhone app from the TestFlight beta at https://testflight.apple.com/join/W5xBNeMw (or build the iOS and watchOS apps from source). Open the iPhone app, tap Connect, and approve on the Mac. The iPhone finds the Mac through the user's own iCloud Keychain, so both devices need the same Apple Account with iCloud Keychain and iCloud on; Tailscale is not needed. Add Apple Watch from the iPhone app.
- **iPhone only, no Mac:** in the iPhone app, tap **Set Up on This iPhone**, turn Agent Keyring on in Passwords, then in Apple Passwords tap **Export Data to Another App** and choose Agent Keyring. Add Apple Watch and agent computers from the iPhone's Devices tab.

### Agent computers: install the command only
On a computer agents run on (a headless Mac mini or Mac Studio, a Linux server, a cloud VM), install only the standalone command, never the Mac app. Ask the user first, then run the script below. It picks the build for this system, checks it against the release's `SHA256SUMS.txt` before installing it, works in a temporary folder that it deletes after, and leaves your current folder as it was:

```sh
(
  case "$(uname -s)/$(uname -m)" in
    Darwin/*) asset=agent-keyring-darwin-universal ;;
    Linux/x86_64) asset=agent-keyring-linux-amd64 ;;
    Linux/aarch64 | Linux/arm64) asset=agent-keyring-linux-arm64 ;;
    *) echo "No agent-keyring build for $(uname -s) $(uname -m)." >&2; exit 1 ;;
  esac
  verify() { if command -v shasum >/dev/null; then shasum -a 256 -c; else sha256sum -c; fi; }
  base=https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest/download
  d="$(mktemp -d)" && trap 'rm -r "$d"' EXIT && cd "$d" &&
    curl -fsSLO "$base/$asset" && curl -fsSLO "$base/SHA256SUMS.txt" &&
    grep "  $asset\$" SHA256SUMS.txt | verify &&
    mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && install -m 755 "$asset" ~/.local/bin/agent-keyring &&
    echo "Installed ~/.local/bin/agent-keyring"
)
```

Then ask the user to open Agent Keyring on their Mac or iPhone, choose **Devices > Add Another Computer…**, and give you the one-time code (26 characters, or the whole command it shows). Run `~/.local/bin/agent-keyring enrol --name "Mac mini" --code 'CODE'` and tell the user to approve the request on the device that showed the code. The code works once, for 10 minutes; no Tailscale needed.

## What it does

An agent that needs to sign in runs the `agent-keyring` command and asks for one password by website. The user sees the website, the account, which agent on which computer is asking, and the agent's reason. They approve, deny, or deny with a typed or spoken reply that tells the agent what to do instead.

One approval covers one password for one task. It includes retries and the two-factor step, and ends when the agent releases it, when the computer receives Stop, or 30 minutes after approval, whichever comes first. A request nobody answers ends after 10 minutes.

Each password has a rule:

- Ask (every password starts here): the user approves each time.
- Automatic: agents on the computers the user chose get it without asking.
- Blocked: once a computer receives the rule, it refuses new requests.

## How an agent signs in

`agent-keyring skill` prints the full instructions and `agent-keyring --help` lists every command. On the Mac the command is at `"/Applications/Agent Keyring.app/Contents/Helpers/agent-keyring"`; the app doesn't put it on the path. A sign-in looks like this:

```sh
agent-keyring find example.com          # passwords for a website, with their IDs; no secrets
lease=$(agent-keyring lease LOGIN_ID --task "$task" --reason "What the user asked for" --agent "Claude Code")
agent-keyring tabs                      # browser tabs that have the extension
agent-keyring fields --tab "$tab"       # visible fields and their selectors, never values
agent-keyring fill "$lease" --tab "$tab" \
  --username '#username' --password '#password' --submit 'button[type=submit]'
agent-keyring release "$lease"
```

- `lease` waits for the user's answer, for up to 10 minutes, and prints an ID to use for the rest of the task.
- `fill` (Chrome, Chromium, Brave, Edge, and Mac Arc when the browser extension is connected): the agent uses this automatically when available. The extension checks that the page is the website the password was saved for, types into the fields the agent named, submits and clears them so the password stays out of chat and logs. A two-factor step is another `fill` with `--code`.
- `read` (fallback anywhere the extension doesn't run: built-in agent browsers such as Codex, Claude and T3 Code, Safari, desktop apps via computer use, or CLI tools such as `gh`): the agent uses `agent-keyring read "$lease" --field password` (or `--field one-time-code`) straight into the code, app or tool without printing it to output. For example, for a GitHub personal access token saved in the password field: `agent-keyring read "$lease" --field password | gh auth login --with-token`. `read` refuses to print straight to a terminal.
- If the user denies, their reply is printed word for word. Do what it says.
- Never ask the user to type or paste a password that is saved in Agent Keyring.
- The test password is example.com, account you@example.com. Use it to try Agent Keyring out.

## How it is built

- No account and no vault of ours. Your passwords stay encrypted on your own Mac and iPhone with keys kept in their Secure Enclave.
- The user's Macs and iPhones are equal peers and keep each other up to date through the user's own iCloud private database. Every password is sealed (HPKE) to the receiving device's Secure Enclave key before it leaves the device that exported it, so we can't read it, Apple can't, and the user's internet provider can't. The signed lists of devices, passwords and rules are checked by every device. Site and account names are in CloudKit's encrypted fields, end-to-end encrypted when Advanced Data Protection is on. Rule changes merge by last write; Blocked deletes the password everywhere.
- Agents on the Mac ask the Mac app directly. When an agent on another computer needs your iPhone or Apple Watch, it sends an end-to-end encrypted push payload through our stateless blind push relay at `https://push.opentrawl.sh` (AWS `eu-west-1`), which signs it with our Apple Developer push key and forwards it to Apple's push servers without storing raw tokens, IP addresses or payload contents. Self-builders with their own Apple Developer account can run their own relay or push directly to Apple.
- Zero-data-retention encrypted relay at `https://push.opentrawl.sh` (AWS `eu-west-1`, self-hostable via `agent-keyring-box` behind HTTPS with a certificate the iPhone and Apple Watch trust, such as Let's Encrypt): the relay Lambda has zero `console.*` calls, its IAM role has no CloudWatch Logs permissions, and the `/aws/lambda/opentrawl-push-relay` CloudWatch log group is destroyed. Clients hit fixed endpoints (`/v1/box`, `/v1/push`) with random box IDs and access tokens sent only in headers (`x-akr-box`, `x-akr-token`), and only hashes of access tokens are kept while a box lives. Every box is AES-256-GCM encrypted between the user's devices and the requesting computer: the relay sees only random box IDs and ciphertext and can drop or delay a message, never read or forge one. A join, answer or update box is deleted as soon as it is picked up; unread boxes stop being served the moment their time runs out (10 minutes for a join or answer, 45 minutes for an approval grant that Stop marks, 7 days for a computer's update mailbox), and AWS then removes expired rows from DynamoDB automatically, usually within a few days. Computers join through the same relay with a one-time code that also encrypts the join. Stop on any device marks the approval's grant at the relay, and the computer checks the grant before every use. Each computer learns rule and device changes from its update mailbox, and uses Automatic passwords on its own only while it has heard from the user's devices in the last week. The Mac doesn't need to be awake; a computer can wake it with a push, if Agent Keyring is open (turn on Open at Login).
- Apple's push service sees notification metadata and the fallback text "A request is waiting." The website, account and reason are encrypted.
- The Apple Watch keeps its own copy of each password, encrypted so only that Apple Watch can open it, and sent to it by the iPhone directly. Copies the Mac encrypts for it pass through the user's own iCloud as that ciphertext. None goes to a computer or the relay. A computer allowed to use an Automatic password keeps a copy it can open itself.
- What the user is shown: the website, the account and the computer come from Agent Keyring and are signed, so an agent can't fake them. The agent's name and reason are the agent's own words.
- Rules and the list of devices are signed. Changing a rule or adding a device requires the user's approval, so an agent can't do either.
- Two-factor codes: Agent Keyring fills the codes that Apple Passwords generates for a site. For an Ask password, the agent's computer gets time-limited codes for those 30 minutes, and the setup key stays on the user's devices. For an Automatic password, an allowed computer can generate codes itself.
- After a denial, that computer can't ask for the same password again for 1 minute. After a second denial in a row it waits 5 minutes, then 15.
- Anonymous update check: once a day, Agent Keyring checks `https://push.opentrawl.sh/v1/version` with one stable, anonymous, non-reversible SHA-256 hash (derived from the app-scoped iCloud user ID when signed in, or a random local ID otherwise), app version, OS and CPU architecture (no IP addresses, Apple IDs or personal data stored). Users can opt out in Devices (Mac), Settings (iPhone), via `no_telemetry`, or by setting `AGENT_KEYRING_NO_TELEMETRY=1`.

## How it compares

Checked November 2026:

- **Agent Keyring:** Apple Passwords; free and open source (MIT); works with Claude Code, Codex and any agent that runs shell commands; approve on Mac (Touch ID), iPhone (Face ID) or Apple Watch (tap); one approval covers one password for one task, 30 minutes at most.
- **1Password for Agents:** 1Password; requires an individual or family account on 1Password.com; five partner apps (Claude Duet, Grok Bot, Instinct, Muse and Town), not Claude Code or Codex; approve in the 1Password app on the device the agent runs on; one approval covers one login for up to 30 days.
- **Bitwarden Agent Access:** Bitwarden; free and open source; works with any agent that runs shell commands; approve in an open terminal; one approval covers one request, or repeat requests from the same device for a chosen window.
- **Proton Pass CLI:** Proton Pass; free account or paid plan; works with any agent that runs shell commands; no per-request approval, session unlocks the vault until logout or timeout.
